messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Chain Ensembles
parts:
Peter brought up the question of how to interface ensemble samplers with Stan, but if you step back the real question is how to interface ensembles of chains in Stan (in the simplest case an ensemble sampler is a single chain with all of other walkers just part of the proposal mechanism; it's easy to assign a single chain to each walker and then have them mix in the proposal stage, but this just generates more chains, not more samples).  So, just how do we want people to do inference with multiple chains?  

One option is to interleave the chains (carefully as to preserve detailed balance) and then do inference on the mega-chain.  My concern here is that the mega-chain might have a very weird autocorrelation structure (aliasing, single-frequency modes) that would invalidate most autocorrelation estimators (can't cut off the lags past the first zero anymore).

The other option is to calculate expectations from each chain, and then average them together using the ESS as weights.  This approach is more awkward for the user, as the averaging of the expectations need not commute with other manipulations (marginalization, etc).

Thoughts?

Once we've decided on this it won't be hard to modify command appropriately (for example, adding a chain index as a sampler parameter for ensemble methods or just having multiple output files).

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
I'm not sure, but just in general I think it's important for our paradigm to be that we return to the user a set of simulations which he or she can use to represent the posterior distribution.  Calculating expectations is fine but that's just one thing that can be done with the simulations, I don't think it should be the paradigmatic activity.  And I really really don't want to be handing out weights--not unless there's a really really good reason to do so!
A

Regular MCMC samples are dependent and we aggregate them.

To put it another way, imagine the goal was to compute expectations.  In that case, any weighting of chains would be valid.  Equal weighting might not be the most efficient but it is still kosher.

One option is to do different rates of thinning of different chains.

A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
But is an aggregation of samples equivalent to a reversible Markov chain?  For example, if we

1) randomly sample a walker
2) evolve it 
3) take the evolved state as a sample

then we can consider the process as a mixture of Markov transitions.  Because each transition converges to the same stationary distribution, the mixture will, too.

But if we

1) evolve all walkers
2) append all evolved states as samples

then I don't think we have the same guarantee.  I'm not so much worried about convergence but the behavior of the autocorrelation estimators, in particular when/how we can terminate the lags in computing the ESS.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
On 5/24/13 12:54 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> But is an aggregation of samples equivalent to a reversible Markov chain?
I don't think so.

> For example, if we
>
> 1) randomly sample a walker
> 2) evolve it
> 3) take the evolved state as a sample
>
> then we can consider the process as a mixture of Markov transitions. Because each transition converges to the same
> stationary distribution, the mixture will, too.
Right.

> But if we
>
> 1) evolve all walkers
> 2) append all evolved states as samples
>
> then I don't think we have the same guarantee. I'm not so much worried about convergence but the behavior of the
> autocorrelation estimators, in particular when/how we can terminate the lags in computing the ESS.

I don't think we do, either.

For convergence and ESS, we want to keep the ensemble members separate.

For inference and posterior estimation, we want to throw them all together.
Andrew also wants to randomize the thrown-together samples to protect vs. client
code that might do something non-random, like take the first 200.

If the ensemble goes long enough, then the effect of just laying the
ensemble members end to end will diminish, so it should be the same in
the limit. But we hope to stop long before that happens! So what would
happen is that we'd underestimate autocorrelation by crossing ensemble
member boundaries.

- Bob

would involve splitting into 2, splitting into 3 (or 4), splitting
into 4 (or 8), and so on.  No idea how to do it, but it does remind

We can use DFT methods to compute relevant sums, but I don't think they're quite appropriate for Rhat.  The problem is that they give you they don't give you split partitions (first n/2 samples, last n/2 samples) but rather offset partitions (all even-indexed samples, all odd-indexed samples) so you don't get the same sensitivity to drift as you do in the split-Rhat case.  Unless I'm looking at it incorrectly?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
While waiting for acid_tests to run I spent some time looking through the ensemble literature, eventually going back to the original Goodman and Weare paper on which emcee is based.  Unlike the emcee paper (on the arXiv, glosses over waaaaaay too many details) Goodman and Weare treat the ensemble sampler as a Markov chain on the product space pi cross pi .... pi cross pi, and explicitly note that any the sequence of any particular walker is very much NOT a Markov chain.  In the end, though, they get tricky.  When comparing ESS between a single chain and the ensemble, they collapse the ensemble at each sample by averaging each walker to produce f_{i} = sum_{j} f (x_{ij}), where i indexes time and j the walkers.  They then compare ESS/accuracy using both 1D chains.

So one possibility for Stan is to output not output the full product space in samples.csv (or have multiple output files, one for each walker) and then have bin/print produce any summary stats using the above method.  Any nonlinear expectations needed by the user can be accommodated by adding transformed parameters in the original model.

Thoughts?

    I see, so it's not how to compute split R-hat, but a new R-hat that

parts:
On 6/13/13 12:54 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> While waiting for acid_tests to run I spent some time looking through the ensemble literature, eventually going back to
> the original Goodman and Weare paper on which emcee is based. Unlike the emcee paper (on the arXiv, glosses over
> waaaaaay too many details) Goodman and Weare treat the ensemble sampler as a Markov chain on the product space pi cross
> pi .... pi cross pi, and explicitly note that any the sequence of any particular walker is very much NOT a Markov chain.

Right. Their equation (5) states (but does not explain why)
that for J walkers at iteration i, you have:

p(x_{i,1},...,x{i,J}) = p(x_{i,1}) ... p(x_{i,J})

I'd like to understand why. It seems wrong to me given
that x_{i,j} depends on x_{i-1,j} and also at least two
other points, other x_{i-1,j'} and x_{i-1,j''}.

> In the end, though, they get tricky. When comparing ESS between a single chain and the ensemble, they collapse the
> ensemble at each sample by averaging each walker to produce f_{i} = sum_{j} f (x_{ij}), where i indexes time and j the
> walkers. They then compare ESS/accuracy using both 1D chains.

In section 3, they seem to be restricting attention to estimating
posterior expectations means.

> So one possibility for Stan is to output not output the full product space in samples.csv (or have multiple output
> files, one for each walker) and then have bin/print produce any summary stats using the above method. Any nonlinear
> expectations needed by the user can be accommodated by adding transformed parameters in the original model.
> Thoughts?

We want to do full Bayesian inference, so just averaging over
walkers j isn't going to help us because the posterior
variance will be too low. But, if that can compute a reasonable
effective sample size that we could use with all the samples,
that could work.

But if each walker itself isn't a Markov chain, then we can't
even just use one chain. So I'm not sure what we can do with
the "samples."

- Bob

parts:
> Right. Their equation (5) states (but does not explain why)
> that for J walkers at iteration i, you have:
>
> p(x_{i,1},...,x{i,J}) = p(x_{i,1}) ... p(x_{i,J})
>
> I'd like to understand why. It seems wrong to me given
> that x_{i,j} depends on x_{i-1,j} and also at least two
> other points, other x_{i-1,j'} and x_{i-1,j''}.

Yup, each point in the ensemble depends on each other -- that's why the individual sequences are not Markov chains. But if you treat the ensemble as a state, {x_{0, j}, …, x_{i, j}, … x_{I, j}} then the distribution of the ensemble is preserved by each move. Basically you're parameters are the parameters of the full state and you're just Gibbs sampling when you update one of the walkers.

> In section 3, they seem to be restricting attention to estimating
> posterior expectations means.
Which, to be fair, is about all you can do with MCMC samples.

> We want to do full Bayesian inference, so just averaging over
> walkers j isn't going to help us because the posterior
> variance will be too low. But, if that can compute a reasonable
> effective sample size that we could use with all the samples,
> that could work.

But you don't use the posterior variance of that average. You average x_{j} = 1 / I \sum_{i} x_{ij}, and the sequence { x_{j} } becomes a valid Markov chain. You compute your expectations, variances, ESS, and MCSE from those averages. In fact it's actually more conservative than treating each chain as independent and weighting the samples by the individual chain ESSs.

> But if each walker itself isn't a Markov chain, then we can't
> even just use one chain. So I'm not sure what we can do with
> the "samples."

If you just took one walker and threw everything else out, then you'd have a Markov chain. If you repeated the same process with each walker you'd have something that looked like a Markov chain but together they'd be correlated and so you couldn't treat them independently. By averaging you get around the correlations, but become sensitive to chains that haven't converged (I think you can get around this by using the median).

Basically, you can't use each individual walker as a separate draw. But if you map ( x_{0, j}, …, x_{i, j}, … x_{I, j} ) -> x_{j}, say via an average or a median, for a given time index j then you get a sequence of draws that is a proper Markov chain.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
> Why is the average of the J walkers a Markov chain? If
> mu[i] is the average at i, I can't see how to formulate
>
> p(mu[i] | mu[i-1])
>
> Is there something general that says a transform of a Markov
> chain is a Markov chain? If so, that'd explain why both the
> average and the projection to one walker form Markov chains.

Just consider the multivariate case: you have a Markov chain sampling from some p(x1, x2). You can transform to p( x2 ) = int dx1 p(x1, x2) at each state, so that { x2 } are valid draws from a Markov chain for p( x2 ).

The proof is straightforward. Let T be a Markov transition with invariant density pi(x1, x2). Then by definition

pi(x1, x2) = int dx1' dx2' T (x1, x2 | x1', x2' ) pi(x1', x2').

Integrating both sides with respect to x2 gives

int dx2 pi(x1, x2) = int dx2 dx1' dx2' T (x1, x2 | x1', x2' ) pi(x1', x2')

or

pi(x1) = int dx1' [ int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x1', x2') / pi(x1') ] pi(x1')

pi(x1) = int dx1' [ int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x2' | x1') ] pi(x1')

Where

T(x1 | x1') \equiv int dx2 dx2' T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') pi(x2' | x1')

is a valid Markov transition for pi(x1).

Neal talks about the general case in his ensemble paper, and the intuition is really nice. The marginalized transition first samples x2 from the condition distribution p(x2 | x1) and then performs a transition on the space (x1, x2) before marginalizing back to just x1. It's also how HMC works, where x2 is the momenta, x1 the position, and T(x1, x2 | x1', x2') the Hamiltonian flow + Metropolis correction.

You can readily generalize the proof to include changes of variables x1, x2 -> f(x1, x2) (where f(x1, x2) might be the average or the median), and the same reasoning holds for the ensemble where you consider the state space x = {x1, …, xi, … xI}.

> I don't see how you can estimate posterior variance from
> the mu[i], though. It seems to me that the variance of
> the chain of mu[i] will be lower than that of the component
> walkers.

Right, but you only use the mu[i] to compute the expectation of mu. If you want the variance then you have to compute var[i, j] in each walker and average that. While this method does account for the correlations in a systematic way it is terribly inflexible.
> P.S. Thanks for trying to explain this all to me.
No worries at all. If people didn't push me to explain I'd get in the habit of handwaving instead of whipping up little proofs like that and understanding it better myself. Keep me on my toes!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
parts:
>> I don't see how you can estimate posterior variance from
>> the mu[i], though. It seems to me that the variance of
>> the chain of mu[i] will be lower than that of the component
>> walkers.
>
> Right, but you only use the mu[i] to compute the expectation of mu. If you want the variance then you have to compute var[i, j] in each walker and average that. While this method does account for the correlations in a systematic way it is terribly inflexible.

Actually, this is exactly the behavior we want!  The variance of the means will indeed shrink, which means the MCSE will also shrink.  But that is the desired behavior -- if the walkers are independent then the MCSE will decrease by 1 / n_walkers, giving MCSE = var / (ESS * n_walkers).  The full power of the samples is preserved.

This is exactly what I'm worried about. And not
just for ensemble methods.

We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
we only report n_eff for the mean. What's our
certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

We can calculate theta^2 in a single sample, but not

Agreed. The only issue is that all three require knowing the expectation of interest a priori.

> This is exactly what I'm worried about. And not

>
> We report posterior sd and posterior quantiles, but
> we only report n_eff for the mean. What's our
> certainty on the posterior quantile and sd estimates?

I'm not sure about the quantiles, but you can compute the variance of the variance and define a MCSE the same as for the mean. In practice, however, the uncertainty o the variance isn't as critical -- it's the uncertainty of the posterior uncertainty and second-order in some sense.

> We can calculate theta^2 in a single sample, but not
> variance or sd or quantiles, because they depend on
> multiple samples. In comparing systems, Matt had
> been using theta^2 for all variables theta of interest
> to get a handle on how well posterior variance was being
> estimated.

Right -- technically the variance is a function of the data and an unknown constant (the mean). It can be calculated via the expectations of theta and theta^{2}, however, which would be straightforward to implement in both the single state and ensemble schemes.

> Other expectations, like event probabilities, can be pretty
> easily calculated by defining variables using indicator
> functions. These should have their uncertainties calculated
> properly.

Here's the way I see the grand scheme of things. One of the great features of MCMC is that the samples can be transformed or marginalized trivially, without changing their validity. That means you can run your sampler and still have valid inference even if you decide that you're interested in different expectations. On the other hand, this flexibility requires the user to compute ESS themselves. We can handle the calculations automatically, provided the user define the desired expectations a priori. This leave three approaches

One Stage Stan:

All expectations have to be defined in the model or transformed parameters. We run the model, compute mean, variance, ESS, and MCSE automatically and report those summary statistics.

One Point Five Stage Stan:

We compute the summary statistics automatically as above, but store the intermediate samples in case an expert user wants to change the expectations.

Two Stage Stan:

Sampling and post-processing are two completely different stages, and we rewrite bin/print to be less reliant on the Stan format and assume little more than a csv.

Currently, Stan uses the middle strategy. One Stage Stan would be more user friendly but slightly more annoying for expert users. Of course, it wouldn't be hard to make the approach customizable.
